name: Barnabas

seo.title: Saint Barnabas the Apostle: his life, Paul, Mark and his death
seo.description: Barnabas in plain words: the Son of Encouragement who vouched for Paul, his quarrel over Mark, his feast day, his tomb on Cyprus and the myths.

band.lede: The Son of Encouragement. He vouched for Saul when the church feared him, and gave young Mark a second chance.

picture.alt: A detail of an altarpiece by Fra Angelico: Barnabas, a balding man with short grey curls and a white beard, looks to the right inside a gold halo. He wears a pale pink cloak over a deep blue robe with a gold collar, and holds a red book against his chest. Behind him are green hills and a pale sky, and at the left edge a page of an open book.

who: Barnabas was a Levite from Cyprus named Joseph. The apostles called him Barnabas, Son of Encouragement. When the church in Jerusalem feared Saul, he vouched for him. He taught the new church at Antioch with Saul, then made the first missionary journey with him. They parted over Mark, whom Barnabas would not give up.

tidbits.text: Up to Cyprus, Luke writes “Barnabas and Saul”. After Paphos it is mostly “Paul and Barnabas”. At Lystra and in Jerusalem, Barnabas comes first again.
Acts tells of no miracle by Barnabas alone. At Iconium, it says, the Lord enabled him and Paul “to perform signs and wonders”.
A story of the 400s says he carried a copy of Matthew's Gospel, and laid it on the sick wherever he went: “it immediately made a cure of their sufferings.”

cite.text: Acts of Barnabas, Ante-Nicene Fathers, volume 8

tidbits.text: By the 1500s the old calendar had slipped ten days behind the sun. His day, 11 June, had become the longest day of the year. Hence the old rhyme: “Barnaby bright, the longest day and the shortest night.”

facts.label: Born
facts.text: On **Cyprus**, into a family of **Levites**, the tribe that served in the temple. No one recorded the year.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Joseph**, his own name. Older English Bibles call him **Joses**. **Barnabas**, the name the apostles gave him, which Acts explains as **Son of Encouragement**. Where the name really comes from is disputed. In Italian he is **Barnaba**, in Spanish **Bernabé**.

facts.label: Home
facts.text: **Jerusalem**, in the first church. Then **Antioch** in Syria, where he taught with Saul.

facts.label: Family
facts.text: His cousin was **John Mark**. Mark's mother, Mary, had a house in Jerusalem where the church gathered to pray.

facts.label: Work
facts.text: He worked for his own living, as Paul did. Acts does not name his trade.

facts.label: Journeys
facts.text: With Paul: **Cyprus**, then **Perga**, **Pisidian Antioch**, **Iconium**, **Lystra** and **Derbe**, in what is now Turkey. Then back to **Cyprus**, with Mark.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: The Bible does not say. Later accounts say he died a martyr at **Salamis**, on Cyprus: stoned, and his body burned. The OCA's life of him puts it about the year 62.

facts.label: Buried
facts.text: A tomb near **Salamis** was said to be his when it was found in **488**, with a copy of **Matthew's Gospel** in it. The **Monastery of St Barnabas** stands near the site.

facts.label: Wrote
facts.text: Nothing in the Bible. The *Letter of Barnabas* bears his name, and Tertullian thought he wrote Hebrews: see Often misquoted.

typeNote: The test sets him opposite Paul. He brought Saul to the apostles when the church still feared him, and later wanted to give young Mark a second chance when Paul would not. John Chrysostom put the two side by side: “the one was more tender and indulgent, but this one more strict and austere.”

west.text: **Barnabas the Apostle**, a **Catholic** memorial. Also the **Church of England**, which keeps it as a Festival, the **Episcopal Church**, and Lutherans in the **Missouri Synod** and the **ELCA**.

east.text: The **Apostle Barnabas of the Seventy**, for the **OCA**, on the same day as the apostle Bartholomew.
The **Coptic** Church, on 21 Kiahk in its own calendar: the martyrdom of Barnabas, one of the Seventy.

feasts.note: The *Roman Martyrology* of 1916 keeps him on 11 June, and so did Rome's new calendar of 1969. Churches on the old calendar keep 11 June 13 days later, on 24 June.

said.lede: Luke, Paul and the Fathers, in their own words.

quotes.q: Barnabas was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and faith, and a great number of people were brought to the Lord.
quotes.who: Luke, in Acts, when Barnabas came to Antioch

quotes.q: James, Cephas, and John—those reputed to be pillars—gave me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, so that we should go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcised.
quotes.who: Paul, on the visit to Jerusalem he made with Barnabas

quotes.q: he was one of the seventy, and a fellow-worker of Paul
quotes.who: Clement of Alexandria, about 200, who calls him “the apostolic Barnabas”

cite.text: Clement of Alexandria, Stromata, Book 2, chapter 20

quotes.q: “Son of Consolation” is his appellation, whence also he makes himself easy of access to the man.
quotes.who: John Chrysostom, on why it was Barnabas who took Saul to the apostles

cite.text: John Chrysostom, Homilies on Acts, Homily 21

quotes.q: With the exception of St. Paul and certain of the Twelve, Barnabas appears to have been the most esteemed man of the first Christian generation.

moments.when: The first days of the church
moments.title: The field
moments.text: The first believers in Jerusalem shared everything they owned. Those who had land or houses sold them and brought the money to the apostles. Acts names one of them. Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus, “sold a field he owned, brought the money, and laid it at the apostles' feet.” The very next story is of Ananias and Sapphira, who sold land too, kept back part of the money and lied about it. John Chrysostom saw why Luke put them in that order: he “first mentions him who performed the virtuous deed”.

cite.text: Acts 4:32 to 5:3; John Chrysostom, Homilies on Acts, Homily 12

moments.title: He vouched for Saul
moments.text: Saul had hunted down the followers of Jesus. Now, after the road to Damascus, he came to Jerusalem and tried to join the disciples, “but they were all afraid of him, not believing that he was a disciple.” Barnabas took him to the apostles. He told them how Saul had seen the Lord on the road, and how he had spoken boldly at Damascus in the name of Jesus. So Saul stayed with them, and moved about freely in Jerusalem.

moments.title: The grace of God
moments.text: Believers scattered by persecution reached Antioch. Some began to tell Greeks about Jesus too, and a great number believed. The church in Jerusalem sent Barnabas to see. “When he arrived and saw the grace of God, he rejoiced and encouraged them all to abide in the Lord with all their hearts.” Still more people came to the Lord.

moments.title: He went to find Saul
moments.text: Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul. He found him and brought him back to Antioch. For a full year the two met with the church and “taught large numbers of people.” It was at Antioch that the disciples were first called Christians. When a prophet foretold a famine, the church sent relief to the believers in Judea “with Barnabas and Saul.” They came back with Barnabas's cousin, John Mark.

moments.title: Set apart
moments.text: Barnabas headed the list of prophets and teachers at Antioch. While they were worshipping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, “Set apart for Me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.” After more fasting and prayer, they laid their hands on the two and sent them off. Mark went with them as their helper.

moments.title: From Salamis to Paphos
moments.text: They sailed first to Cyprus, where Barnabas came from. At Salamis they preached in the synagogues. They crossed the whole island to Paphos. There the proconsul, Sergius Paulus, “summoned Barnabas and Saul because he wanted to hear the word of God.” A sorcerer named Elymas tried to turn him from the faith. Saul, “who was also called Paul”, told him he would be blind for a time, and mist and darkness came over him. The proconsul believed. When they sailed on to Perga, Mark “left them to return to Jerusalem.”

moments.title: Taken for Zeus
moments.text: At Lystra, Paul healed a man who had been lame from birth. The crowd shouted, “The gods have come down to us in human form!” They called Barnabas Zeus, and Paul Hermes, “because he was the chief speaker.” The priest of Zeus brought bulls and wreaths to the city gates, to offer sacrifice to them. Barnabas and Paul tore their clothes and rushed into the crowd, and could hardly stop them. Soon after, men from Antioch and Iconium turned the crowd, and Paul was stoned and left for dead. He got up, “And the next day he left with Barnabas for Derbe.”

moments.title: Elders in every church
moments.text: They went back the way they had come, through the towns that had driven them out. They encouraged the new disciples to keep the faith. In each church they appointed elders, “praying and fasting”. Home at Antioch in Syria, they gathered the church and told how God “had opened the door of faith to the Gentiles.”

moments.title: The council
moments.text: Men from Judea came to Antioch teaching that Gentile believers must be circumcised to be saved. Paul and Barnabas argued sharply with them, and the church sent the two to Jerusalem. After Peter spoke, “The whole assembly fell silent as they listened to Barnabas and Paul describing the signs and wonders God had done among the Gentiles through them.” The apostles and elders agreed with them. Their letter to the Gentile believers called the two “our beloved Barnabas and Paul”.

moments.title: “Even Barnabas”
moments.text: At Antioch, Peter used to eat with Gentile believers. When men came from James, he drew back, afraid of the circumcision group. Paul tells what followed: “The other Jews joined him in his hypocrisy, so that by their hypocrisy even Barnabas was led astray.” Paul opposed Peter to his face, in front of them all. Acts does not tell this story. We have only Paul's side of it.

moments.title: The parting
moments.text: Paul wanted to go back and visit the believers in every town where they had preached. Barnabas wanted to take Mark. Paul thought it best not to, “because he had deserted them in Pamphylia and had not accompanied them in the work.” “Their disagreement was so sharp that they parted company.” Barnabas took Mark and sailed for Cyprus. Paul chose Silas. Here the story in Acts leaves Barnabas.

extras.title: The quarrel over Mark
extras.lede: Barnabas wanted to give young Mark a second chance. Paul would not, and the two friends parted. How it turned out, and what later Christians made of it, each in their own words.

items.title: How it turned out
items.text: Years later Mark was with Paul. Paul sent greetings from “Mark the cousin of Barnabas”, and told the church at Colossae, “If he comes to you, welcome him.” He calls Mark one of “my fellow workers”. From prison, in his second letter to Timothy, he wrote:
items.quote: Get Mark and bring him with you, because he is useful to me in the ministry.

items.title: Who was right? John Chrysostom
items.text: Chrysostom saw two different gifts. Barnabas was the gentler man, Paul the stricter, and each was right for the churches he went to. He would not choose between them:
items.quote: Now which of them advised best, it is not for us to pronounce

cite.text: John Chrysostom, Homilies on Acts, Homily 34

items.title: Still friends? Jerome
items.text: Jerome was quarrelling with an old friend of his own, Rufinus. He pointed him to Paul and Barnabas:
items.quote: We read of Apostles quarrelling, namely Paul and Barnabas who were angry with each other on account of John whose surname was Mark; those who were united by the bonds of Christ's gospel were separated for a voyage; but they still remained friends.

items.title: A later telling
items.text: The *Acts of Barnabas*, a story of the 400s told as if by Mark, imagines the scene. Both men knelt and prayed, and both wept. Barnabas says why he will not leave Mark behind:
items.quote: The grace of God does not desert him who has once served the Gospel and journeyed with us.

cite.text: Acts of Barnabas, Ante-Nicene Fathers, volume 8

words.note: Acts records no words of his alone. He speaks with Paul, and every line below is theirs together. Outside the quiz's own section, every Bible line on this page is from the Berean Standard Bible.

feature.kicker: When the crowd called him Zeus
feature.q: Men, why are you doing this? We too are only men, human like you. We are bringing you good news that you should turn from these worthless things to the living God, Who made heaven and earth and sea and everything in them.
feature.ctx: At Lystra, the priest of Zeus had brought bulls and wreaths to the city gates, to sacrifice to them. Barnabas and Paul tore their clothes and rushed into the crowd, shouting.

quotes.q: It was necessary to speak the word of God to you first. But since you reject it and do not consider yourselves worthy of eternal life, we now turn to the Gentiles.
quotes.who: To the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch, when many there turned against them.

quotes.q: Yet He has not left Himself without testimony to His goodness: He gives you rain from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling your hearts with food and gladness.
quotes.who: More of what they told the crowd at Lystra.

quotes.q: We must endure many hardships to enter the kingdom of God.
quotes.who: To the new disciples, on the way home.

myths.truth: The letter never names its writer. It is old: the Codex Sinaiticus, a Bible copied in the 300s, has it straight after the New Testament. About 200, Clement of Alexandria quoted it as the words of “the Apostle Barnabas”. A century later Eusebius put “the extant epistle of Barnabas” among the rejected writings, and added that such books “may be reckoned among the disputed books”. Jerome says Barnabas “wrote one Epistle, valuable for the edification of the church, which is reckoned among the apocryphal writings.” Scholars today do not think he wrote it. As early as 1890, Arthur McGiffert found that the verdict against it had “become practically unanimous”.

cite.text: Clement of Alexandria, Stromata, Book 2, chapter 6; Eusebius, Church History, Book 3, chapter 25, with McGiffert's note; Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 6; Catholic Encyclopedia, “Epistle of Barnabas”

myths.claim: The *Gospel of Barnabas* is an early gospel that he wrote.
myths.truth: The book known by that name survives in an Italian manuscript now in Vienna, and a Spanish copy is known too. It retells the life of Jesus, and in it Jesus foretells the coming of Muhammad. Lonsdale and Laura Ragg first put the Italian into English in 1907. They found its paper was made in the second half of the 1500s, and its scribe was “a Venetian of the sixteenth or early seventeenth century”. The text itself echoes Dante. It speaks of a jubilee held every hundred years. The Raggs noted that this fits only the years 1300 to 1350. An old list of forbidden books, the so-called Gelasian Decree, names a Gospel of Barnabas, but no copy of that one is known.

cite.text: Lonsdale and Laura Ragg, The Gospel of Barnabas (Oxford, 1907), introduction

myths.claim: Barnabas wrote the Letter to the Hebrews.
myths.truth: Hebrews names no writer. Tertullian, about 200, says “there is extant withal an Epistle to the Hebrews under the name of Barnabas”. Jerome knew three views: it was the work of Barnabas “according to Tertullian”, or of Luke, or of Clement of Rome. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* thinks Tertullian was probably wrong.

cite.text: Tertullian, On Modesty, chapter 20; Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 5; Catholic Encyclopedia, “St. Barnabas”

myths.claim: Barnabas was one of the Twelve.
myths.truth: He was not, though Acts calls him an apostle: “the apostles Barnabas and Paul”. When the Eleven chose a man to take Judas's place, one of the two put forward was “Joseph called Barsabbas”, a different Joseph. John Chrysostom already told his hearers not to mix them up: “I do not think that this is the same with the companion of Matthias”. Clement of Alexandria counts Barnabas among the Seventy, the wider circle Jesus sent out, and Eusebius passes it on: “Barnabas, indeed, is said to have been one of them”. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* calls this “A rather late tradition”.

cite.text: Acts 1:23; 14:14; John Chrysostom, Homilies on Acts, Homily 11; Eusebius, Church History, Book 1, chapter 12; Catholic Encyclopedia

myths.claim: Barnabas founded the Church of Milan.
myths.truth: A tradition says so, and the OCA's life of him tells it: “Saint Barnabas founded the episcopal see at Mediolanum (now Milan)”. Other stories have him preach at Rome and at Alexandria. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* weighs them all: “The traditions are all late and untrustworthy.”

cite.text: OCA, Apostle Barnabas of the Seventy; Catholic Encyclopedia, “St. Barnabas”

circle.name: Paul
circle.text: Barnabas vouched for him in Jerusalem, fetched him from Tarsus, and went with him on the first journey. They parted over Mark. Years later Paul still named him as a fellow apostle.

circle.name: Peter
circle.text: He led the church in Jerusalem when Barnabas sold his field. At Antioch, when Peter drew back from eating with Gentiles, Barnabas followed him, and Paul opposed Peter to his face.

circle.name: John Mark
circle.text: His cousin. Mark went with them as their helper, and left them at Perga. Barnabas took him to Cyprus when Paul would not. Tradition makes him the writer of the Gospel of Mark.

circle.name: Simeon called Niger
circle.text: One of the prophets and teachers at Antioch, with Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen and Saul. Together they laid their hands on Barnabas and Saul and sent them out.

circle.name: Sergius Paulus
circle.text: The proconsul of Cyprus, “a man of intelligence”. He sent for Barnabas and Saul to hear the word of God, and believed.

circle.name: The church at Antioch
circle.text: Jerusalem sent Barnabas to it, and he and Saul taught there for a year. It sent the two with famine relief, then sent them out on their first journey, and welcomed them home.

death.title: How the record leaves him
death.big: The Bible does not say how or when he died. Later accounts say he died a martyr on Cyprus.
paras: Acts leaves him sailing for Cyprus with Mark. A few years later Paul names him as an apostle who still worked for his living. That is the last the Bible says of him.
When Paul, in prison, sends greetings from “Mark the cousin of Barnabas”, Barnabas himself is not named. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* takes this as a sign that he had died by then.
*Britannica* puts it plainly: “Nothing is known for certain about the time or circumstances of his death.”

Later accounts place his death at Salamis, the port where he first preached on Cyprus. The Coptic Synaxarium tells it this way: “They seized St. Barnabas and brutally beat him, then they stoned him and finally burnt his body with fire.” Mark, it says, laid his body in a cave.

In 488 Anthimus, the chief bishop of Cyprus, “claimed to have learned by a revelation” that the grave was near his city of Salamis. He found a body there with a copy of Matthew's Gospel, and took the relics to the emperor Zeno at Constantinople. The find helped the Church of Cyprus keep its independence from Antioch. The *Roman Martyrology* of 1916 says the Gospel was “copied with his own hand”.

later.title: A story of the 400s
later.text: The *Acts of Barnabas* is told as if by Mark. *Britannica* calls it “a 5th-century forgery”. In it, his enemies at Salamis put a rope round his neck and dragged him out of the city. “They burned him with fire, so that even his bones became dust.” Mark and two friends hid the ashes in a cave, “with the documents which he had received from Matthew”.

cite.text: Acts of Barnabas, Ante-Nicene Fathers, volume 8; Britannica

saint.big: Yes. Every church that keeps saints' days honours him, nearly all of them on 11 June.

churches.note: A Festival in the Church of England

paras: He was not one of the Twelve, but the churches call him an apostle, as Acts does. The Orthodox and the Copts count him among the Seventy whom Jesus sent out.
The *Catholic Encyclopedia* credits Paul, Barnabas and Mark with preaching the faith on Cyprus. The finding of his tomb in 488 helped the Church of Cyprus keep its independence.
Rome's book of martyrs, in its 1916 edition, gives his day like this:

quotes.q: By the disciples, he was ordained apostle of the Gentiles with St. Paul, and with him traversed many regions, fulfilling his commission to preach the Gospel. At length he went to Cyprus, where he ennobled his apostolate by a glorious martyrdom.

kin.name: Antony the Great
kin.text: After twenty years alone in the desert he came out, says Athanasius, so settled that his friends were amazed. His face was cheerful, because his soul was at peace.

kin.name: Cuthbert of Lindisfarne
kin.text: Bede found him pleasant and easy to talk to, with a cheerful, soothing way of speaking. Made a bishop, he went back after two years to his island.
